title: Command Line Repetition
text:
2 Accessing and navigating c3se
We will be using the c3se cluster Vera for these labs. If you do not have access yet, or you forgot how to log in, follow the instructions provided in BIO511 to access the cluster.

title: Command Line Repetition
text:
3 Folders and files
In UNIX everything is a file. Therefore, knwoing how to navigate files and directory structures is essential for knowing how to interact with a unix system using the CLI.
Check what directory you are in upon accessing the cluster. This is your home directory and can always be accessed using ~. Check what folders and files are currently in there.

Create a new directory for this course, and a subdirectory for this session.
Create a file in your directory for this session and append the sequence below.
>ACT1 YFL039C SGDID:S000001855, Chromosome VI:53260..54696
ATGGATTCTGGTATGTTCTAGCGCTTGCACCATCCCATTTAACTGTAAGAAGAATTGCAC
GGTCCCAATTGCTCGAGAGATTTCTCTTTTACCTTTTTTTACTATTTTTCACTCTCCCAT

TACTCTTTCTCCACCACTGCTGAAAGAGAAATTGTCCGTGACATCAAGGAAAAACTATGT
TACGTCGCCTTGGACTTCGAACAAGAAATGCAAACCGCTGCTCAATCTTCTTCAATTGAA

CCAGAAGCTTTGTTCCATCCTTCTGTTTTGGGTTTGGAATCTGCCGGTATTGACCAAACT
ACTTACAACTCCATCATGAAGTGTGATGTCGATGTCCGTAAGGAATTATACGGTAACATC
GTTATGTCCGGTGGTACCACCATGTTCCCAGGTATTGCCGAAAGAATGCAAAAGGAAATC
ACCGCTTTGGCTCCATCTTCCATGAAGGTCAAGATCATTGCTCCTCCAGAAAGAAAGTAC
TCCGTCTGGATTGGTGGTTCTATCTTGGCTTCTTTGACTACCTTCCAACAAATGTGGATC
TCAAAACAAGAATACGACGAAAGTGGTCCATCTATCGTTCACCACAAGTGTTTCTAA






Note



What type of file is this? What file ending should you use?


Check how many lines your file contains. Does this make sense?
If we want to look at the sequence we’ve just stored, but without the header, how can we do this?


3.1 Using grep
A common property of DNA sequences that is often interesting is their GC content. Differences in GC content between species and genomic regions can provide insight into genome organisation and can influence both biological and technical properties of the DNA. Try calculating the GC content for your sequence.






Tip



Remember your friend |.




3.2 BLAST
The sequence you looked at above is from the gene ACT1, which is quite conserved in eukaryotes and encodes actin. This sequence was collected from the Saccharomyces Genome Database (SGD) and is an S. cerevisiae reference sequence. But let’s say that we want to look at this gene/protein in other organisms too.
The ACT1 sequence of another species has already been saved for you in the directory for this course (collected from NCBI, which you will work with later). To get to this directory, use the following path: /cephyr/NOBACKUP/groups/n2bin_gu/ from here, navigate to the BIO514 introduction folder. Copy the file more_actin.fa to your own workspace.
To find out what species this sequence originates from, we can use BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool). This is a widely used program to compare nucleotide or protein sequences to a database of known sequences. By identifying regions of local similarity, homology, functional predictions of unknown sequences and of most likely organisms of origin can be determined. To use BLAST, we can see if it is already loaded by default in our environment. If this is not the case, check its availability on the server & load it into your own environment. Check that this has worked correctly.






Tip



Environment modules can be accessed using the module command.


Once you have done this, it is time to run the tool. Your query is a nucleotide sequence, which you’ll want to compare to a remote nucleotide database. Think about which flags you will have to use, and where you wish to store the output. Look at your results. What species are you working with? Store this information in the header of the file.


3.3 NCBI
Append the contents of more_actin.fa to your original sequence file. Once you’ve done this, you can delete more_actin.fa. Don’t forget that deleting files is a permanent action on the server. There will be no prompt to double-check you really want to delete anything, unless you modify this behaviour using flags.
Next up, try adding more organisms’ ACT1 gene to your comparison. We can use NCBI, or the US National Center for Biotechnology Information, to do this. This platform provides a variety of useful databases and resources for bioinformatics. Navigate to the ‘gene’ database on the NCBI website to look for this gene in a couple of other species. Once you have found some other DNA sequences you want to include, add them to your sequence file. Make sure the headers make sense! Do the same thing, but for protein sequences too.


3.4 CLUSTAL
Now that all your DNA sequences are in one file, you can use the multiple sequence aligner CLUSTAL to visualize which parts are the most conserved. There are different programs in the Clustal family (e.g. ClustalW and Clustal Omega, both available online too), using different algorithms but serving the same purpose.
Clustalo is not by default loaded in your environment and is also not among the available modules on the server. A third way to work with a tool on the cluster is using a container. A container is a packaged software environment that contains a program and everything it needs to run. Using containers helps avoid problems with missing dependencies and makes analyses more reproducible as well. A container has already been built for you and can be found under ‘images’ in the BIO514 folder.   ::: {.callout-tip} For this course we will use apptainer/singularity containers. :::


3.5 Submitting jobs to compute nodes
So far, you’ve been working in your login node. This is a shared entry point used my many users at the same time. This has been perfectly fine, as it is intended for light, low-resource, interactive tasks. Running CLUSTAL will be a bigger job though. For jobs such as these, it is good practise to instead book compute cores. You request dedicated computing resources for your job. While your job is running, those cores are reserved for you, and you are free to run more demanding analyses without affecting other users.
To run jobs in this way, you should submit them to the scheduler, here SLURM. C3se provides a manual to do this. Write a simple job script. Start with the shebang, followed by the project account information (not sure? Try running projinfo in the terminal). Specify the right partition. One CPU core, 10 minutes, will be enough. Then write your command to execute the clustalo script you have just created.
Before submitting your job, check to make sure both scripts have the right permissions. Then it is time to submit your job! Don’t forget you can check on its status too.






Report - Task 2



Take a look at the output and compare between the nucleotide and amino acid alignments. Interpret the results. Do you observe conserved regions? How are they indicated?




3.6 Sequencing data
Aside from fasta, another very common bioinformatic filetype is fastq, containing quality information as well as sequence information. On the Canvas page for this course, under ‘labs’, ‘introduction’, you can find paired-end Illumina sequencing reads in fastq format.
Upload these files to your working directory. Unzip the files and check their contents. Does the format make sense to you?
Raw sequencing reads often contain low-quality bases, adapter sequences, or other technical artefacts that can interfere with downstream analyses. For this reason, reads are commonly pre-processed before mapping or assembly.
fastp is an all-in-one tool that performs both quality control and filtering/trimming of sequencing reads in a single step. It is not available on the cluster, but you can build a container yourself!
We will do this using apptainer. Start by installing Apptainer on your Linux system (or WSL on Windows):
sudo apt install apptainer
If this works, skip the rest of this section and move on to creating your definition file. If not, your system does not provide Apptainer through the package manager. In that case, it can be built from source:
git clone https://github.com/apptainer/apptainer.git
cd apptainer
git checkout v1.3.1
./mconfig
make -C builddir
sudo make -C builddir install
Apptainer is written in Go, so if you do not have this yet, you might need to install it first:
wget https://go.dev/dl/go1.22.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz
sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.22.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz
echo 'export PATH=/usr/local/go/bin:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
You might also need uidmap if it is not yet installed:
sudo apt install uidmap
Next, create a definition file to build your container. This file describes which base system to start from, what software to install and how the container should behave when run.

Create a file which you can call fastp.def with the following contents:
Bootstrap: docker
From: mambaorg/micromamba:1.5.8

%post
   micromamba install -y -n base \
      -c conda-forge \
      -c bioconda \
      fastp && \
   micromamba clean --all --yes

%environment
   export PATH=/opt/conda/bin:$PATH

%runscript
   exec fastp "$@"
Build the container
apptainer build fastp.sif fastp.def
Once your container is built, copy it to the HPC! :::{.callout-tip} When the container is executed, it behaves as if you are running fastp. So any arguments you pass to the container are forwarded to fastp – similarly to how you ran clustalo previously. :::
Run fastp on your samples. The default settings are fine, but feel free to make changes. How to run this tool is well described in this BIO511 tutorial. How much of your data was filtered out?

title: Command Line Repetition
text:
4 Mapping to a reference genome
For most analyses, your individual sequencing reads will have to be mapped/aligned to a reference genome next. A lot of different mapping tools exist. One of these, already available on the cluster, is called BWA (Burrows-Wheeler Aligner). Consisting of different algorithms, the one most suitable for your samples is called BWA-MEM.
Before running this tool, a reference genome is necessary. As the name of your samples implies, you will need a mouse reference. You can get this from ENSEMBL, another large resource providing various genomes and tools, using the following command:
wget https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-113/fasta/mus_musculus/dna/Mus_musculus.GRCm39.dna.primary_assembly.fa.gz

4.1 Indexing
Many tools require indexing of large files like this one. In this case, it allows the aligner to more efficiently and quickly find where a read could map to our reference. Creating an index only has to be done once for any given file. Make sure not to run this task on your login node as it is more demanding.


4.2 Mapping
Once you have created your index, it is time to try running BWA-MEM. The output of this tool is a .sam file though, which is plain-text and human-readable, but very large and inefficient to store/process. Usually these are not stored directly, but instead immediately converted to a .bam file, containing the same information in binary format – smaller and faster to read and write. We can use SAMtools, also available on the cluster as a module, to do this. Pipe the output of bwa mem directly into samtools view, to convert it to a .bam file, and then pipe this to samtools again, to sort the file, which would be required by most downstream tools, allowing easier access to specific genomic regions.


4.3 Interpretation
Now we can check the success of our alignment using flagstat, and stats, both also a part of samtools. We can use samtools view to take a look at the header of the SAM file as well. In the top of the file, all lines start with ‘@’. This is part of the header. The second part contains detailed information about your mapping. Do you understand the different columns?
There are many other tools available to perform mapping. Find a second tool, either available on the cluster or from elsewhere, and compare the results.






Report - Task 2



Take a look at the output of both your mapping tools and compare. How well did they perform? Which one do you prefer? Why?

5 Report
Write a short report answering the questions in both tasks. You can include screenshots of your screen if you would like. This does not have to be long, half an A4 page should suffice!

title: Variant Calling
text:
In this practical you will try to run a basic variant calling workflow to try and find and interpret variants in adapted yeast populations.


A variant is a fairly broad genomics term. In general, variants an be divided into…
Short variants:

Single Nucleotide Variants (SNVs/SNPs)
Multi Nucleotide Variants (MNVs/MNPs)
Insertions and Deletions (Indels)

Large/Structural Variants:

Tandem and interspaced duplications
Inversions
Translocations
Copy Number Variants

But these terms are often not well-defined and definitions may overlap depending on who you ask.



We often talk about variants being either germline or somatic. Germline variants are present in all cells in an induvudual (i.e. passed from parent to child), whereas somatic variants only occur de-novo in some cells in an individual (eg. in a tumor). Naturally, these terms make very little sense when talking about single-cellular organisms, especially when they divide by binary fission. An alternative way to think about it is that germline variant calling compares sequence data from a sample with a reference, whereas somatic variant calling compares sequence data from a sample to sequence data from another sample AND a reference.



In this practical you will use data from a large-scale experimental evolution dataset where a yeast strain (YPS128) was exposed to several environmental stressors. We will use data from populations exposed to Arsenite and Rapamycin. The population are allowed to adapt for ~300 generations (50 cycles) by repeatedly re-pinning to fresh media when the populations reach stationary phase (~3 days). The fitness of each population can be traced over time using the Scan-o-Matic platform, where the growth-rate of each population can be tracked. The growth rate of a yeast population is a good indicator of the overall fitness.
By sequencing both the founder and adapted populations, we can then look at differences in the sequences to find variants that influence adaptation to a given environment. This is where you come in. You have been provided with raw paired-end Illumina short-reads (.fastq, founder and adapted) and an annotated reference assembly of the YPS128 genome. Your task is to run a basic variant calling workflow to identify interestng variants in these populations.
The data has been provided in two .tar.gz files in canvas.

yps128.reference.tar.gz - All needed reference files (plus a few extras).
<SAMPLE>.reads.tar.gz - Raw reads for a given sample, both founder and adapted poplations.







Note



Pick one sample to start with. When you finish you can go back and pick another one, preferably from a different environment.

title: Variant Calling
text:
2 Basic Workflow






Important



The reads are paired-end and should be processed as such.








Important



You should perform the QC, mapping, and post-processing steps both for the adapted AND the founder populations.








Note



Make sure to name the intermediate files in a way so that you can remember what you have done to them (e.g. X_R1.trimmed.fq.gz, X_R2.trimmed.fq.gz).



2.1 Raw data QC and sanity check
It is usually a good idea to take a look at the raw data before you start working on it, to notice and possbily fix any problems before you go ahead with an analysis.

Run fastqc on the raw reads. Are there any problems? What is the adapter content like?
Run fastp tpo trim adapter sequences and low-quality bases from the reads.
Finally, run fastqc on the trimmed reads again. Can you notice a difference?







Note



You can use MultiQC to combine several FastQC reports (and reports from other tools)




2.2 Mapping
We will be using BWA-MEM2 for mapping. There are many other short-read mappers available, but BWA-MEM2 is by far the most commonly used.

Use bwa-mem2 to map your trimemd reads to the reference (YPS128.genome.fa). The output should be in the .sam format.







Important



Make sure to add -R "@RG\tID:AS_A2\tSM:AS_A2\tPL:ILLUMINA" to your BWA-MEM2 arguments (Replace AS_A2 with the id of your sample, appending _founder to the founder population). We will need these read groups for out downstream analysis.








Note



The YPS128.genome.fa has been indexed for you, and all files should be included in the .tar.gz you were provided.




2.3 Mapping post-processing
Before variant calling we need to do a few things to our mapped reads.

Use samblaster to mark duplicates in the .sam files from bwa-mem.
Use samtools sort to sort reads by coordinate.
Use samtools calmd to calculate MD and apply BAQ
Use samtools index to generate .bai indexes for the final .bam files.







Note



Make sure the final output from samtools is compressed bam (-Ob) to keep file sizes down. If you are piping data from one samtools command to the next you should use uncompressed bam except for the last step.








Question



Why is it important to mark duplicates when calling variants?








Question



What does MD and BAQ mean?




2.4 Short variant calling
For short variant calling we will use freebayes in pooled continous mode on both the founder and adapted populations at the same time. This will allow us to later identify true de-novo variants in the adapted population.

Use freebayes with the final indexed .bam files from the post-processing step. Make sure to include both the founder and adapted populations.
Use bcftools index to generate a .tbi index for your .vcf.gz file.







Important



Make sure to pass both the adapted and founder .bam files as input to freebayes, as we will use both wen filtering.








Note



An alternative approach could be to use GATK Mutect2, a somatic variant caller, with the founder as the “normal”. You may need to tweak the settings quite a bit to get it to work well with our data. The default settings in Mutect2 are quite strict, and you may need to be a bit more lenient to find variants. This would aslo require a different filtering approach.








Question



Why do we run freebayes in pooled continous mode?








Question



Take a look at your output .vcf.gz. Can you see any interesting variants?




2.5 Variant annotation and filtering
As you may have noticed, it’s pretty difficult to draw any conclusions from your raw .vcf.gz generated above. To help you find interesting variants we will apply some basic filtering and generate a simplifed table of variants.

Use snpeff to annotate your .vcf.gz using the provided snpeff.config and yps128 genome.
Use bcftools norm to split multiallelic variants as they will interfere with downstream filtering.
Use bcftools +fill-tags to add the FORMAT/VAF tag to your .vcf.gz.
Use bcftools index to index the final .vcf.gz
Use snpsift extractFields to generate a simplified .tsv from your final .vcf.gz. Include the chromosome, position, reference and alternate alleles, gene name, VAF in the founder and adapted populations, and coverage (depth) in the founder and adapted populations.







Note



If you still have too many variants you can filter out downstream, intronic, and intergenic variants when annotating with snpeff.








Question



What does VAF mean in a variant calling context?








Question



Take a look at your final .tsv. Can you find any interesting variants?








Question



Load your final .vcf.gz in IGV. You will need to load YPS128.genome.fa as a genome and add a track for YPS128.all_feature.gtf. Look at the variants you find interesting. Do they look ok?








Question



Based on your understanding of the underlying biology, look at regions where you would expect to see variants. You can also load your unfiltered .vcf.gz to look for variants that were filtered out.








Question



The bcftools commands’ help pages mention .bcf (it is also in the name). What is this format? How does it differ from .vcf.gz?




2.6 Structural variant calling
Sometimes, short variants do not tell the whole story. It can also be helpful to take a step back and looking at a larger scale. In this practical we will be looking for copy number variations.

Use cnvkit batch to generate a whole-genome copy ratio profile of your adapted .bam, with your founder .bam as the normal.







Note



Our data was generated using whole-genome-sequencing (WGS). Make sure cnvkit knows this.








Question



Can you see any interesting variations in the whole-genome copy ratio profile? Do they make sense given your environment and your understanding of the underlying biology?
